wstep: This card describes freezing butter according to the NCHFP, at 0 °F (−18 °C) or lower.

akapity: Freeze only high-quality butter made from pasteurized cream.
Cottage cheese, ricotta and cream cheese do not freeze well; cream cheese combined with heavy cream can be frozen for later use in dips or icing.
According to Clemson University (HGIC), do not freeze yogurt, sour cream, buttermilk or sweet cream, because their texture changes (in cream the fat separates).

Shape it into squares or portions and wrap them tightly in aluminum foil, transparent film or freezer paper, or seal them in moisture-vapor resistant containers; this protects against other odors and freezer burn.
You can overwrap the original carton.
Use packaging that is moisture- and vapor-resistant, durable and leakproof, and does not become brittle or crack in the cold.
Pack tightly, leaving as little air as possible, and press as much air as possible out of freezer bags before sealing.
Label each package with the name of the product, any added ingredients, the packaging date, the number of servings or amount, and the form, such as squares or portions.
Freeze at 0 °F (−18 °C) or lower.
To speed up freezing, set the freezer to −10 °F (about −23 °C) or lower about 24 hours in advance.
Add to the freezer at one time only as much food as will freeze within 24 hours, because overloading slows freezing and lowers quality.
Spread new, warm packages with space between them, and stack them close together only once they are frozen.
According to Clemson University (HGIC), freeze as quickly as possible, because slow freezing forms large ice crystals that damage cells on thawing.
According to the same source, a refrigerator freezing compartment that cannot hold 0 °F (−18 °C) or is opened often is for short-term storage only.
Keep the freezer at 0 °F (−18 °C) or lower, because at higher temperatures food loses quality faster; keep a freezer thermometer in it and check it often.
Freezing does not kill all bacteria, yeasts and molds; it only stops them multiplying while the food is held at 0 °F (−18 °C) or lower, and after thawing they can multiply again.
Food kept constantly at 0 °F (−18 °C) stays safe indefinitely, and the recommended storage times are for quality only: after them the food is still safe but lower in flavor, color and texture.
Freezer burn, grayish-brown leathery spots, is surface drying of poorly wrapped food caused by air; it does not make food unsafe, it only lowers quality, and the burned spots can be cut away.
For best quality, keep to the shorter time and use the oldest packages first.
At 0 °F (−18 °C) or lower, the recommended shelf life of butter is 6–9 months.
According to the NCHFP, thaw butter, eggs, milk and cheese in the refrigerator and then use them as fresh.
Thaw dishes and products containing eggs or dairy in the refrigerator or in the microwave.
Do not keep perishable food out of the refrigerator for more than 2 hours, or for more than 1 hour when the temperature is above 90 °F (about 32 °C).
Food is safe while it stays frozen, but once it thaws and warms above 40 °F (about 4 °C), bacteria present before freezing can start to multiply.
During a power outage keep the freezer closed: according to the FDA, a full freezer holds its temperature for about 48 hours, a half-full one for 24 hours.
According to the NCHFP, food stays frozen longer if the freezer is full, unopened, in a cool place and well insulated; it can be covered with blankets, away from the compressor.
JarAtlas rule (cautious) after a freezer failure: throw away any package that has no ice crystals and is above 40 °F (about 4 °C), or that you cannot check.
The FDA also says to throw away perishable food that has been at room temperature for 2 hours or more, or 1 hour when it is above 90 °F (about 32 °C) outside.
